Murlo builds a Luddite point-and-click alone, Zhou Yichen's Game Boy elegy for a grandmother goes to metal, and a print profile finds William Chyr bending Escher into Manifold Garden. Plus Rebounder, a lunar platformer inked in halftone.









By Jamin Warren • 1 Oct 2026

Something Beautiful at Aviva Studios (courtesy of Factory International)











 











 














Hi hi hi Reader,

So, this week, Yaloo Lim at CalArts invited me as a visiting artist, and I had a wonderful time interfacing with students. I gave a lecture on experimental ambition in games and shared some direction for future game makers and artists (More memoirs! Shorter games!)

One student, Nikko, asked a specific question about my taste; it was apparent I had an interest in minimalism in interactions. I hadn't quite thought about it that way, but if you look at my Playlist [https://www.killscreen.com/r/d300870b?m=REDACTED] picks each week, I am deeply interested in games with a limited mechanical palette with an expansive visual and narrative appeal. I think there's so much to experiment with in games as a medium and with a single interaction system; why make something needlessly complex? Anyway, maybe I need to write a manifesto?

Great stuff this week: a Manchester producer making a point-and-click alone, an artist pressing a Game Boy elegy into metal, a Miami film collective selling a game in the language of cinema.

Thank you to the 59 of you who signed up this week (especially Laura, who became a paid member.) You pushed Killscreen past 5,000, which is a lot of people who want to hear about strange games. Welcome in.

----------------------------------------

 


This Week's Feature


Murlo Builds a World You Can Play [https://www.killscreen.com/r/bfc6bffa?m=REDACTED]

Chris Pell spent a decade reading dance floors. Now he is building a Luddite point-and-click alone, for one player at a time, with an album hidden inside it.

Something Beautiful (via Steam)

William Blake trusted almost no one to make his books. He wrote the poems, etched the plates, printed the pages, and colored them by hand (with his wife, Catherine, of course), so that word and image arrived together as one private cosmology. Murlo, the Manchester producer and illustrator born Chris Pell, works in a similar spirit. Across a string of releases on his own label, Coil Records, he has been building a single world one record at a time: the dreary sprawl of Coil City, the forest folklore of Dolos (2019), and the AI-worshipping cult of Puckle (2023), the records arriving with his own graphic novel, sculptures, and lore.

For most of the last decade, Murlo made his living the usual way, touring and releasing records. A track synced to an advert changed that. The money bought him time away from playing shows, and for the past two years he has spent it on a game. Something Beautiful, a music-driven, point-and-click adventure he is building alone, sets the spirit of the 19th-century Luddites loose on a broken industrial estate, with an entire album embedded in the world and jukeboxes made of flesh.

It is a move from outdoors to indoors. A DJ reads a room and plays to whoever is standing in front of the decks. A game asks someone, anywhere in the world, to sit alone with a complete, self-contained thing, closer to putting on an LP than to going to a show. At a concert you are rarely fully present. In front of a computer, you might be. A slice of the game ran this spring on the Media Wall at Factory International's Aviva Studios [https://www.killscreen.com/r/3dbfa04e?m=REDACTED], played on a controller he covered in his own 3D-printed sculptures, and Murlo hopes to finish the full game within the year. We spoke about Shepshed, jungle music in a theme park queue, haptics, and why the buttons are under your skin.

The industrial estate in Something Beautiful (courtesy of Murlo)

A game about Guantánamo is being built with its survivor [https://www.killscreen.com/r/2dc92dcf?m=REDACTED]

GTMO 441: Games, Detention, Power (via Biome Collective)

Mansoor Adayfi, held at Guantánamo without charge for 14 years, is co-creating a game about it with Joseph DeLappe and Biome Collective, the team behind Killbox. Detainees used games to survive the camp, and the project starts from that documented practice rather than from empathy tourism.

Theory of Relativity [https://www.killscreen.com/r/8a5e8547?m=REDACTED]

Twisting traditional notions of videogame architecture

William Chyr. Photograph by David McDowell

Chicago artist William Chyr’s Manifold Garden is drawn from M.C. Escher, real-world architects, and Chyr’s own pedigree as a large-scale installation artist. The game’s preoccupation with scale and perspective has been refined over a four-year development cycle into a legitimately disorienting experience: one that’s half physics lesson and half existential question.

I don’t know any other game developers who got started as a juggler. William Chyr was studying Physics and Economics at the University of Chicago when he first joined a local circus group. “Which, coming from physics, isn’t that far off, within the math physics engineering population there’s a higher proportion of jugglers versus the general population,” he said. “Not really sure why.”

Behind Control Resonant's ads: Harmony Korine's EDGLRD [https://www.killscreen.com/r/10e1481d?m=REDACTED]

EDGLRD's campaign for CONTROL Resonant (via Instagram)

Remedy's biggest marketing campaign ever came out of EDGLRD, Harmony Korine's Miami collective, which made Aggro Dr1ft with game-engine artists and decided cinema's future looks more like games than film. The footage it posted the day CONTROL Resonant shipped is a filmmaker's shop selling a game in its own terms.

Rebounder, coming to Steam in 2027 (via Aggro Crab)

Rebounder is the first signing for Aggro Crab's new publishing label: a lunar worksite of 500-plus hand-built screens, drawn like a sci-fi comic that went through a cheap press. It lands on Steam in 2027.
